## Optional extension

This page is optional. You can compare the pairwise form of the ODE with the mean-field form. Implement both versions and see how they differ in computational cost and in the resulting dynamics. The mean-field form is much faster for large populations and gives the same trajectories.
:::

## Pairwise form

You can write the right-hand side in two ways ([The Kuramoto Model](kuramoto-model.qmd) and [The Order Parameter](order-parameter.qmd)):

$$
\dot\theta_i = \omega_i + \frac{K}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N \sin(\theta_j - \theta_i)
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\dot\theta_i = \omega_i + K r \sin(\psi - \theta_i).
$$

The pairwise form is straightforward but expensive for large $N$. The mean-field form is cheaper and shows how each oscillator responds to the whole population.

::: {.callout-note}

## Hint

Broadcasting builds the full matrix of differences in one line: `theta[None, :] - theta[:, None]` has entry $\theta_j - \theta_i$ in row $i$, column $j$.

Once both functions exist, switching between them is as simple as changing the ODE function in the `solve_ivp()` call inside the `update_function()` of [Animation](kuramoto-animation.qmd):

```python
sol = solve_ivp(
    kuramoto_ode_pairwise, # Change this to the other ODE function
    (0, dt),
    theta,
    args=(omega, coupling_strength),
    )
```

This is why **modularity** matters. By keeping your code organized and modular, you can swap out one component (like the ODE function) without rewriting the animation code. A modular structure also saves work in the [Kuramoto Assignment](assignment-kuramoto.qmd), where you implement a different model of coupled oscillators, the Millennium Bridge.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

```python
def kuramoto_ode_pairwise(t, theta, omega, coupling_strength=1.0):
    # Row i, column j holds theta_j - theta_i
    diff = theta[None, :] - theta[:, None]
    dtheta_dt = omega + coupling_strength / len(theta) * np.sin(diff).sum(axis=1)
    return dtheta_dt


theta, omega = initialize_oscillators(100, seed=1)
print(np.allclose(
    kuramoto_ode_pairwise(0, theta, omega, 2.0),
    kuramoto_ode_meanfield(0, theta, omega, 2.0),
))  # True
```
:::

## Computational cost

::: {.callout-note}
## Exercise

Time both ODE functions with `%timeit` (or `time.perf_counter()`) for $N = 100$, $1000$ and $5000$. How does the cost grow with $N$ in each case?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

The pairwise version builds an $N \times N$ matrix of phase differences, so one evaluation costs $O(N^2)$ time and memory. The mean-field version computes one complex mean, which costs $O(N)$. Going from $N = 1000$ to $N = 5000$ should multiply the pairwise time by roughly 25 and the mean-field time by roughly 5. Both give the same trajectories up to round-off.
:::
